body_markdown:
As if Africa doesn’t have enough problems, the continent is going through a bitter divorce. For the past 25 million years, a chunk of its eastern landmass the size of India has been trying to move out—in fact, toward India—creating the East African Rift, a 3000-mile-long seam from the Red Sea down to Mozambique. At the southern end of this fissure are some sleeping volcanoes, including Mount Kilimanjaro and the Ngorongoro Crater.


You have to be up early if you want the Ngorongoro to yourself for an hour or two before the traffic picks up. The Tanzanian rangers open the steep incline road at 0600, and after camping in the rim clouds among marauding water buffalo, we were the third vehicle down, turning left at the bottom where the others had hooked a right. Puttering across the savanna blissfully alone, we suddenly stopped with a squeak of brakes; two huge bull elephants had appeared from the morning mist, and as our cameras auto-fired with a rattling *tika-tika-tika!* , they loped to within a dozen yards of us before tromping on. It was my favorite moment in Africa, made possible by a 30-year-old Toyota Land Cruiser.


Aaron Robinson


The British were happily pumping Land Rovers into Tanganyika before the territory achieved independence in 1961. To this day, you can see a few battered Series doing duty in the towns, but out on the Serengeti, where everything must fight to avoid extinction, Land Rover sealed its doom when it quit producing the old Defender in 2016. What might be called the Land-cruiserozoic Period set in.


Aaron Robinson


Toyota replaced its 40-series workhorse with the equally formidable 70-series in 1984, and that truck, having had no fewer than five different wheelbases and 23 different engines (no combination of which came to the U.S.), is still in production. Authuman, our Tanzanian guide, said most of the safari operators in nearby Arusha rely on 70-series, many of them shipped secondhand from the Middle East and modified by Indian-owned companies to varying degrees of quality. The frames and bodies get stretched to hold more clients, and the roofs are raised and fitted with fiberglass pop-tops that provide shade during the long hours of game spotting. By comparison, our almost stock and stripped Troopy—a single rear side door was added in back—looked properly vintage with its flat, beige fenders and round lights.


The roads in northwest Tanzania are so rutted and broken that 15 to 20 years is about all most drivers can handle before their bodies give out, said Authuman, before he turned over the helm to me for a day on the Serengeti. First, I drove us to see hippos grunting and mouth-jousting in a river. Then we came upon a lion pride playing tug-of-war with a wildebeest taken down in the night. The Cruiser’s 4.2-liter diesel straight-six was born to this job, sending smooth torque to the long-throw five-speed and tractoring through the bush at a low, fuel-sipping rpm.


Aaron Robinson


A safari driver spends all day picking paths up the ever-changing trail that won’t toss the customers, many of whom are standing up through the hole in the roof. How Authuman can both drive and spot leopards in trees from a quarter-mile remains a trade secret. I rode the three planes back to LA dreaming of my own 70-series but gave up when I found that good ones are $40 grand. Oh well, as with everything else we saw on this trip, the 70 is probably something best left in Africa.
